summary: Comments on the TCP Big Window option described in RFC 1106, pointing to a problem with it. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone looked at the idea of sending bigger batches in RFC 1106 and said, "wait, there is a problem with this."

questions: problem with tcp big window option
why is tcp window size limited
how does tcp handle packet reordering
subtitle: Why expanding TCP's window size breaks packet reordering safety.

tldr.problem: RFC 1106 proposed expanding TCP's transmission window from 16 bits to 30 bits to support high-bandwidth, high-delay networks, but did not increase the sequence number space.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC points out that when windows grow much larger than the sequence number space, a packet lost in the network and delayed long enough can be reused in a later cycle, causing TCP to accept duplicated old data as new.
tldr.outcome: The proposal works only in networks that never reorder or delay packets, not in the general Internet which must handle both.

today: RFC 1110 is historic and was replaced by RFC 6247.

sections.title: The Window Size Limitation
sections.content:
TCP uses a 16-bit window field to say how many bytes the receiver can accept. This limits the window to 65,536 bytes. In old networks this was plenty. However, high-bandwidth links (like satellites) combined with long delays create a "bandwidth-delay product" that means many megabytes can be in flight at once. RFC 1106 proposed using a 30-bit window to solve this.

The problem is that TCP sequence numbers are 32 bits long. With the original 16-bit window, a sequence number wraps around only after 65,536 round-trip times, making each number unique. Expanding the window to 30 bits breaks this guarantee.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP uses numbers to label each byte. The window says how many bytes can go out at once. Making the window big without making the number space big causes confusion.

sections.title: Why This Breaks in the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet can lose packets, reorder them, and duplicate them. If a packet is lost in the network and then delayed for many round-trip times, it may arrive after its sequence number has wrapped around and is now in use again. With a 30-bit window and 32-bit sequence numbers, a reappearing old packet can arrive while its sequence number is valid in the current window, fooling TCP into accepting it as new data. This corrupts the data stream.

RFC 1106 assumes a simple satellite network that either delivers packets in order or loses them outright, never reordering. Such a network would not have this problem. But the general Internet has always had the ability to reorder packets, and likely always will.
sections.plainLanguage: In the Internet, packets can get stuck and arrive late with old numbers. If window numbers recycle too fast, a stuck packet looks like a new message instead of an old one.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: RFC 1110 concludes that the RFC 1106 approach cannot be used for general Internet use. A proper solution would need to increase the sequence number space along with the window, not just expand the window. This is a critical design insight about how TCP's basic mechanism depends on the balance between window size and sequence number space.
sections.plainLanguage: To make windows bigger, you have to also make the number space bigger, or old packets will cause trouble.
